words.definition: To explain something in greater detail or develop it more fully.
words.example: When the professor asked her to elaborate, she gave three more reasons for her claim.
words.mnemonic: e-LABOR-ate: it takes labor to add all those extra details.

words.definition: A figure of speech that describes one thing as if it were another.
words.example: Calling the crowded city a jungle is a metaphor for its chaos and danger.
words.mnemonic: META (beyond) + PHOR (carry): it carries meaning beyond the literal words.

words.definition: Vivid descriptive language that makes readers picture sights, sounds, or feelings.
words.example: The poem's imagery of frost and bare branches made the winter feel real.
words.mnemonic: IMAGE-ry: language that hangs pictures in the gallery of your mind.

words.definition: To describe something as less complex than it really is, losing accuracy.
words.example: Saying the war had one single cause is to oversimplify a tangled history.
words.mnemonic: OVER + SIMPLE: you make it TOO plain, stripping away the messy truth.

words.definition: To understand or interpret something wrongly.
words.example: Don't misconstrue my silence as agreement; I simply had nothing to add.
words.mnemonic: MIS (wrong) + CONSTRUE (interpret): you construct the wrong meaning.

words.definition: To twist or change something so it no longer represents the truth.
words.example: The tabloid distorted her quote until it meant the opposite of her intent.
words.mnemonic: DIS + TORT (twist, like 'torque'): to twist a thing out of shape.

words.definition: The method and practice of teaching.
words.example: Her pedagogy relied on probing questions rather than lectures to spark thinking.
words.mnemonic: PED (child, Greek 'paidos') + AGOGY (lead): leading children, i.e. teaching.

words.definition: Having or showing deep, wide knowledge gained from study.
words.example: The erudite old librarian could cite sources on nearly any subject you raised.
words.mnemonic: E-RUDE-ite: not rude at all, but so polished by learning it's the opposite.

words.definition: Relating to serious academic study or the people who pursue it.
words.example: The journal only publishes scholarly articles backed by rigorous research.
words.mnemonic: SCHOOL-arly: it sounds like school, the natural home of academic work.

words.definition: Memorizing by repetition without grasping the meaning.
words.example: He learned the times tables by rote, chanting them until they simply stuck.
words.mnemonic: ROTE sounds like 'wrote': you wrote it a hundred times to burn it in.

words.definition: To improve someone morally or intellectually through instruction.
words.example: She chose documentaries that would edify her children, not just entertain them.
words.mnemonic: EDIFY is kin to EDIFICE (a building): you build up someone's mind.

words.definition: To give someone knowledge or understanding they lacked before.
words.example: A quick chat with the mechanic enlightened me about what the rattling noise meant.
words.mnemonic: EN + LIGHTEN: to switch on the light so someone can finally see clearly.

words.definition: To fix an idea or habit in someone through persistent repetition.
words.example: Their coach worked to inculcate discipline through daily, unvarying drills.
words.mnemonic: IN + CULCATE (Latin 'calcare', to stamp with the heel): stamp it in.

words.definition: To merge two distinct things into one, treating them as the same.
words.example: Critics conflate the author with her narrator, blaming her for his ugly views.
words.mnemonic: CON (together) + FLATE (blow, as in 'inflate'): blow two things into one.

words.definition: To question someone closely and often aggressively.
words.example: Detectives interrogated the suspect for hours, pressing him on every small detail.
words.mnemonic: INTER + ROGATE (Latin 'rogare', to ask): to keep asking, insistently.

words.definition: A condition or stipulation attached to an agreement that must be met.
words.example: She agreed to fund the trip, with the proviso that he keep every receipt.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'pro-VISA' — a visa granted only if you meet certain terms.

words.definition: Useful for teaching something or providing helpful knowledge.
words.example: Watching the master carpenter fix his own mistake was more instructive than any lecture.
words.mnemonic: Contains 'instruct' — something that instructs you leaves you knowing more.

words.definition: Relating to schools, academic study, or formal education.
words.example: His scholastic record earned him a scholarship to the university.
words.mnemonic: 'Scholar' hides inside it — a scholar's world is the world of the classroom.

words.definition: Keen good judgment and the ability to make wise decisions.
words.example: The old farmer predicted the storm days early, a sagacity born of decades outdoors.
words.mnemonic: A 'sage' has it — sage + acity = the quality of a wise sage.

words.definition: A deep, clear understanding of the true nature of something.
words.example: Her years as a nurse gave her real insight into why patients hide their pain.
words.mnemonic: 'In' + 'sight' — the power to see into a thing, past its surface.

words.definition: To think about something carefully and for a long time.
words.example: He sat by the window to contemplate whether to accept the job across the country.
words.mnemonic: 'Con-TEMPLE-ate' — picture sitting quietly in a temple, deep in thought.

words.definition: A sharp or witty reply, especially one answering a previous remark.
words.example: Stung by the insult, she fired back a rejoinder so cutting the room went silent.
words.mnemonic: RE-JOIN-der: you RE-JOIN the verbal fight with a quick comeback.

words.definition: To deny, contradict, or declare something false.
words.example: The evidence was so overwhelming that not even his rivals dared to gainsay it.
words.mnemonic: 'Gain' + 'say' — old English 'gain' meant 'against,' so to speak AGAINST.

words.definition: To argue against or attempt to prove wrong.
words.example: The lawyer produced receipts to controvert the witness's claim that no money changed hands.
words.mnemonic: CONTRA (against) + VERT (turn) — turn against a statement to challenge it.

words.definition: Able to be clearly shown or proven to be true.
words.example: There is a demonstrable link between the new policy and the drop in traffic accidents.
words.mnemonic: 'Demonstrate' + '-able' — able to be DEMONSTRATED for all to see.

words.definition: The central or most important point of a problem or issue.
words.example: We can debate details later, but the crux is whether we can afford the project at all.
words.mnemonic: Latin for 'cross' — the crux is where all the roads of an argument CROSS.

words.definition: To prove a person or argument to be wrong.
words.example: One well-designed experiment was enough to confute the theory the professor had defended for years.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'CON-fute' — a CON artist gets exposed when you fute (foil) his story.

words.definition: Having no practical relevance because it is already settled or hypothetical.
words.example: Once the flight was cancelled, arguing over the best seat became entirely moot.
words.mnemonic: A cow's 'MOO' about spilled milk — pointless to keep debating it.

words.definition: Only slightly connected to the main subject; peripheral.
words.example: Her question was so tangential that the speaker gently steered the discussion back on track.
words.mnemonic: Think of a TANGENT line just grazing a circle — barely touching the main point.

words.definition: A system in which people advance based on talent and achievement.
words.example: In a true meritocracy, the best coder gets promoted, not the boss's nephew.
words.mnemonic: 'Merit' + 'cracy' (rule) — power that is earned by merit alone.

words.definition: A system of government in which citizens vote to choose their leaders and shape decisions.
words.example: After decades of dictatorship, the nation finally embraced democracy and held its first free elections.
words.mnemonic: From Greek 'demos' (people) + 'kratos' (power) — literally 'power of the people.'

words.definition: An organized community or state with a structured form of government.
words.example: Ancient Athens was a small but remarkably influential polity in the Greek world.
words.mnemonic: From Greek 'polis' (city-state) — a city organized into a single governed body.

words.definition: A political community founded for the collective good of everyone in it.
words.example: The former colonies joined together to form a commonwealth of independent states.
words.mnemonic: 'common' + 'wealth' = wealth and well-being held in common by all.

words.definition: The health, happiness, and good fortune of a person or group.
words.example: The charity works tirelessly to protect the welfare of orphaned children.
words.mnemonic: Think 'fare well' — to wish someone fares well is to care for their welfare.

words.definition: The practice of donating money and effort to help those in need.
words.example: Her philanthropy funded three new hospitals across the poorest regions of the country.
words.mnemonic: Greek 'philo' (love) + 'anthropos' (humankind) = love of humankind.

words.definition: Unselfish concern for the well-being and happiness of others.
words.example: Diving into the icy river to save a stranger was an act of pure altruism.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'alter' (other) — putting the other person first.

words.definition: The quality of being kind, caring, and wishing to do good.
words.example: The old shopkeeper's benevolence showed in the free meals he quietly gave the poor.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'bene' (good) + 'volent' (wishing) = well-wishing.

words.definition: Generous giving of help or money to people in need.
words.example: Every December they donate warm coats to charity for the city's homeless.
words.mnemonic: Think 'cherish' — you cherish others by giving freely to them.

words.definition: Willingness to give freely, more than is expected or required.
words.example: His generosity was legendary; he never once let a friend pay for dinner.
words.mnemonic: 'Gener-' as in 'generate' — a generator that keeps producing gifts to give.

words.definition: Extremely generous in giving; lavishly openhanded.
words.example: The billionaire made a munificent gift of one billion dollars to the university.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'magnificent' — a magnificent, big-hearted giver.

words.definition: Generous giving of gifts or money, often by someone wealthy or powerful.
words.example: Thanks to the patron's largesse, every artist in the village received a monthly stipend.
words.mnemonic: Contains 'large' — giving in large, sweeping amounts.

words.definition: Devoted to relieving suffering and promoting the welfare of others.
words.example: Doctors flew into the war zone on a humanitarian mission to treat the wounded.
words.mnemonic: Built on the root 'human' — caring for all human beings.

words.definition: A deep sympathy for the suffering of others, with a wish to help.
words.example: Filled with compassion, she knelt beside the weeping child and held her hand.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'com' (with) + 'passion' (suffering) = suffering alongside someone.

words.definition: The ability to understand and share another person's feelings.
words.example: Having lost her own mother young, she felt deep empathy for the grieving boy.
words.mnemonic: 'em' (in) + 'pathy' (feeling) = feeling your way into another's shoes.

words.definition: Feelings of pity and sorrow for someone else's misfortune.
words.example: She sent a handwritten card expressing her sympathy after his father passed away.
words.mnemonic: 'sym' (together) + 'pathy' (feeling) = feeling together with someone.
